title: Journey and Conquest
overview: Deuteronomy chapter 2 details the Israelites' journey through hostile territories as they prepare to enter the Promised Land. God directs them to avoid conflict with certain nations, respecting His sovereign allotment of lands to other peoples such as Esau’s descendants and the Moabites. The chapter recounts the destruction of formidable ancient peoples and culminates in the divine promise and fulfillment of victory over Sihon, king of the Amorites. This chapter emphasizes God’s faithfulness in guiding and providing for His people, His sovereign control over nations, and the importance of obedience to His commands during the wilderness wanderings.
structure:
**Verses 1-5: Divine Instructions Regarding Edom.** The Israelites are commanded to journey northward and pass through the land of Esau without conflict, respecting God’s gift of Mount Seir to Esau.

**Verses 6-12: Respect for Moab and Historical Context of Giants.** God instructs not to distress Moabites, explaining the presence of ancient giants and the succession of peoples in these lands.

**Verses 13-16: Crossing the Brook Zered and the Passing of a Generation.** The chapter marks the end of the wilderness wandering generation and the transition to a new phase under God’s promise.

**Verses 17-23: Instructions Concerning Ammon and Historical Notes on Peoples.** Similar to Edom and Moab, the Israelites are told not to fight Ammon, with historical references to the giants who once inhabited the land.

**Verses 24-37: Conquest of Sihon and the Amorites.** God commands the Israelites to engage in battle with Sihon, promising victory. The chapter concludes with the successful conquest and the boundaries of the land they are to possess.

keyVerses.text: Meddle not with them; for I will not give you of their land, no, not so much as a foot breadth; because I have given mount Seir unto Esau for a possession.
keyVerses.significance: This verse highlights God's sovereign distribution of land among nations and His command for Israel to respect these divine boundaries, underscoring obedience and trust in God's plan.

keyVerses.text: For the LORD thy God hath blessed thee in all the works of thy hand: he knoweth thy walking through this great wilderness: these forty years the LORD thy God hath been with thee; thou hast lacked nothing.
keyVerses.significance: This verse affirms God's providential care and blessing over Israel during their wilderness journey, reinforcing the theme of divine faithfulness and provision.

keyVerses.text: Rise ye up, take your journey, and pass over the river Arnon: behold, I have given into thine hand Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon, and his land: begin to possess it, and contend with him in battle.
keyVerses.significance: This verse marks the transition from peaceful passage to active conquest, demonstrating God's promise of victory and the fulfillment of His covenantal promises.

keyVerses.text: But Sihon king of Heshbon would not let us pass by him: for the LORD thy God hardened his spirit, and made his heart obstinate, that he might deliver him into thy hand, as appeareth this day.
keyVerses.significance: This verse reveals God's sovereign control over the hearts of kings and nations, orchestrating events to accomplish His purposes for Israel.

keyVerses.text: Only the cattle we took for a prey unto ourselves, and the spoil of the cities which we took.
keyVerses.significance: This verse illustrates the complete victory granted by God and the spoils of war, emphasizing God's provision and justice in the conquest.

characters.name: Moses
characters.description: The leader and prophet who receives direct commands from God and instructs the Israelites on their journey and conduct toward neighboring nations.

characters.name: The LORD (God)
characters.description: The sovereign God who directs Israel’s journey, commands respect for other nations’ lands, promises victory over enemies, and provides for His people throughout their wilderness wanderings.

characters.name: Sihon, King of the Amorites
characters.description: The Amorite king who refuses Israel passage, provoking battle and defeat by Israel under God’s command.

characters.name: The Children of Esau (Edomites)
characters.description: Relatives of Israel who inhabit Mount Seir; God commands Israel not to engage them in battle, respecting their allotted land.

themes.description: God’s control over nations, hearts of kings, and the distribution of land is a central theme, showing His authority over history and fulfillment of promises.

themes.theme: Obedience and Respect for God’s Commands
themes.description: Israel’s obedience in avoiding conflict with certain peoples and trusting God’s guidance reflects the importance of submission to divine instruction.
Throughout the wilderness journey, God’s provision and blessing are emphasized, assuring Israel that they lack nothing under His care.
The chapter portrays God’s judgment on hostile nations and the conquest of the Promised Land as part of His covenantal plan for Israel.

historicalContext: Deuteronomy 2 is set during the Israelites’ wilderness wanderings around the late Bronze Age, approximately the 15th century BC. Geographically, the narrative covers regions east of the Jordan River, including Edom (Mount Seir), Moab, Ammon, and the Amorite kingdom of Heshbon. These areas were inhabited by various peoples, some of whom were descendants of Lot and Esau, with whom Israel had complex relationships. The political situation involved tribal nations and city-states, with God directing Israel to respect certain territories while conquering others. The mention of giants and ancient peoples reflects the cultural memory of formidable inhabitants displaced by successive groups.

theologicalInterpretations.description: This perspective emphasizes God's sovereign election and providence in orchestrating Israel's journey and conquest, highlighting the fulfillment of covenant promises and the necessity of obedience to God's commands.

Dispensationalists see this chapter as part of the historical fulfillment of God's promises to Israel, distinguishing the land allotments and divine judgments as literal events that foreshadow future prophetic fulfillments.

Early church interpreters often saw the conquest narratives as typological, representing the spiritual battle against sin and the need for the believer to trust God's guidance and power in overcoming spiritual enemies.

crossReferences.connection: God’s promise to give Israel the land and command to be strong and courageous parallels the instructions and assurances in Deuteronomy 2.
This passage recalls God’s command to Israel not to touch His anointed and to respect the boundaries of Edom and Moab, echoing Deuteronomy 2’s instructions.
The account of Israel’s request to pass through Amorite territory and the subsequent battle with Sihon corresponds directly with Deuteronomy 2’s narrative.
The faith of Israel in crossing the Jordan and conquering enemy lands is commended, reflecting the trust in God’s promises seen in Deuteronomy 2.
The chronicler’s record of battles with giants and Amorite kings complements the historical references to giants and conquest in Deuteronomy 2.

application: Trust God’s sovereign plan even when circumstances require patience and obedience to His timing.
Respect the boundaries God sets in life, avoiding unnecessary conflict and honoring His authority.
Recognize God’s faithful provision in all seasons, giving thanks for His sustaining care.
Step forward in faith to claim God’s promises, knowing He empowers victory over obstacles.
Obey God’s commands fully, understanding that His guidance leads to blessing and success.
Remember that spiritual battles require reliance on God’s power, not human strength.
conclusion: Deuteronomy chapter 2 powerfully illustrates God’s sovereign guidance and provision as Israel journeys toward the Promised Land. The chapter teaches believers to trust in God’s timing, respect His divine allotments, and courageously engage the battles He ordains. Through the historical narrative of conquest and obedience, believers today are reminded of God’s faithfulness to fulfill His promises and the necessity of walking humbly under His authority. This chapter encourages steadfast faith, reverent obedience, and confident reliance on God’s power in every stage of the Christian journey.
timeline: c. 1446 BC - Wilderness Wanderings and Preparation to Enter Canaan

definitions.definition: To interfere or engage in conflict; here it means not to provoke or fight with the Edomites or other nations.
A land or territory granted by God to a people as their inheritance.
Refers to the Anakims and other ancient peoples noted for their great size and strength, often symbolizing formidable opposition.
Goods or valuables taken from defeated enemies during conquest.
Stubbornly refusing to change one’s mind or course of action, as in Sihon’s hardened heart.
